Now we use the tools from Chapters 1–4 on a real study: **66 trainees** in robot-mediated human-service training. The data are de-identified.

## The study in one picture

Trainees practice teaching a child with **discrete trial teaching**. A **robot plays the child**. In a **baseline** rehearsal the robot child cooperates. In a **challenging** rehearsal it shows challenging behavior.

After every rehearsal, the trainee answers three short reports:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A["Rehearsal with<br/>the robot child"] --> B["<b>CB</b><br/>How did the child's<br/>behavior make you feel?"]
  B --> C["<b>SH</b><br/>How do you feel about<br/>how you handled it?"]
  C --> D["Trainer<br/>feedback"]
  D --> E["<b>PF</b><br/>How do you feel<br/>overall now?"]
```

CB and SH are on the same form, right after the rehearsal. PF comes later, after the trainer's feedback. (Question wording is simplified here.)

Each trainee does **6 rehearsals**: 3 baseline and 3 challenging. Each challenging rehearsal shows a behavior with a different **function** (the reason a child might behave that way):

| Function | The robot child… | Why a child might do this |
|----------|------------------|---------------------------|
| **PR**, positive reinforcement | makes demands | to get something |
| **NR**, negative reinforcement | screams and avoids | to escape the task |
| **AR**, automatic reinforcement | repeats itself | the behavior itself feels good |

## Six feelings in every report

| Feelings | Scale | Model we use |
|----------|-------|--------------|
| **Pleasure** (unhappy → happy), **arousal** (calm → excited), **dominance** (controlled → in control) | −4 to +4 (Self-Assessment Manikin) | Linear mixed model ([Ch. 3](03-mixed-models.qmd)) |
| **Confusion**, **frustration**, **boredom** | 1 = not at all … 5 = very strong | Ordinal mixed model ([Ch. 4](04-ordinal.qmd)) |

## The data

```{webr}
#| caption: Load the data
source("R/study_helpers.R")   # small helper functions for this part
d <- load_affect()

head(d[, c("participant_id", "loop_id", "loop_type", "function_class",
           "checkpoint", "pleasure", "confusion")], 6)
```

| Column | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `participant_id` | the trainee |
| `loop_id` | one rehearsal ("loop") |
| `loop_type` | baseline or challenging |
| `function_class` | PR, NR, AR (or baseline) |
| `checkpoint` | which report: `child_behavior` (CB), `self_handling` (SH), `post_feedback` (PF) |
| `pair_position` | which pair of rehearsals: 1st, 2nd or 3rd in the session |
| `pb_order_group` | which order the three challenging behaviors came in (3 orders) |
| `feedback_condition` | the trainer's feedback style: supportive or neutral |

```{webr}
#| caption: How many reports?
nrow(d)                        # 66 trainees x 6 rehearsals x 3 reports
table(d$loop_type, d$checkpoint)
```

Every trainee gave **18 reports**, so their reports are related, just like the sessions in [Chapter 2](02-repeated-measures.qmd). The reports from one rehearsal belong together too:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  P["Trainee<br/>(66)"] --> L["Rehearsal<br/>(6 per trainee)"] --> R["Report<br/>(3 per rehearsal)"]
```

That's why every model in this part has a **random intercept for each trainee**, `(1 | participant_id)`. When we use two reports from the same rehearsal, we add one for each rehearsal, `(1 | loop_id)`.

## A first look

Average of each feeling for each report. Bars show ±1 standard error. Each panel has its own scale, so check the numbers on the axis: boredom barely moves.

```{webr}
#| caption: Average feelings across the three reports
#| fig-height: 6
library(ggplot2)
feelings <- c(sam_feelings, ordinal_feelings)
avg <- do.call(rbind, lapply(feelings, function(v)
  group_means(d, v, c("loop_type", "checkpoint"))))
avg$feeling <- factor(avg$feeling, levels = feelings)

ggplot(avg, aes(checkpoint, mean, colour = loop_type, group = loop_type)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se)) +
  facet_wrap(~ feeling, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("CB", "SH", "PF")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = rehearsal_cols) +
  labs(x = "Report", y = "Average rating", colour = "Rehearsal") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

What stands out: in **challenging** rehearsals, the feelings about the **child's behavior (CB)** are worse than in baseline. In the SH and PF reports, most lines move back toward baseline. The four research questions test these patterns.

## How the ratings are spread

```{webr}
#| caption: Pleasure and confusion about the child's behavior
#| fig-height: 3.5
cb <- subset(d, checkpoint == "child_behavior")
ggplot(cb, aes(factor(pleasure, levels = -4:4), fill = loop_type)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = rehearsal_cols) +
  labs(x = "Pleasure (-4 to +4)", y = "Reports", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

ggplot(cb, aes(factor(confusion, levels = 1:5), fill = loop_type)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = rehearsal_cols) +
  labs(x = "Confusion (1 = not at all)", y = "Reports", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

- **Pleasure** uses the whole scale, so we treat it as a number. Many baseline answers sit at the top (+4), so remember the ceiling.
- **Confusion** is mostly "not at all", with a few higher answers. That's a job for an **ordinal** model.

(Boredom answers of 4 and 5 were so rare that `load_affect()` combines them into "4 or more".)

## The four research questions

In robot-mediated human-service training:

| | Question | What we compare |
|---|----------|-----------------|
| [RQ1](06-rq1-challenging-behavior.qmd) | How does the recipient's challenging behavior influence trainees' affect? | **CB:** challenging vs baseline |
| [RQ2](07-rq2-own-handling.qmd) | How do trainees feel about their own handling of that challenging behavior? | **CB → SH:** does the challenge gap change? |
| [RQ3](08-rq3-after-feedback.qmd) | How do trainees feel after receiving feedback from the trainer? | **SH → PF:** does the challenge gap change? |
| [RQ4](09-rq4-functions.qmd) | How does trainees' affect differ across challenging behaviors with different functions? | **CB, challenging only:** PR vs NR vs AR |

::: {.callout-note}
## How the models were built

Every model on the next pages has:

- **the comparison** that answers the question,
- **the design variables** above, so that when a rehearsal happened, the behavior order and the feedback style can't blur the comparison,
- **random effects** that are as rich as the data allow: each trainee gets their own version of the effect being tested.

The [Model checks](10-model-checks.qmd) page tests these models in several ways: residuals, an ordinal version of the SAM models, the proportional-odds assumption, and different ways of handling order. For pleasure, arousal and dominance, the estimates match the lab's full analysis.
:::
